evidence_quotes.quote: The study is based on a survey of 541 sample households selected from 23 slums of Kolkata, India.

In the city certain slums are authorized by municipality. They are known as notified slums. The unauthorized slums are known as non-notified slums. These slums have been developed mainly by encroaching on government or railway land.

The survey results reveal that around 91 percent of the households reside in notified slums and the rest reside in non-notified slums. The dwellings in the non-notified slums are unauthorized, made of kuccha structure and devoid of any sanitation facility.
We have constructed an index of water, sanitation and drainage. It takes into account the availability and quality of water supply, access to sanitation or toilet and access to drainage.
The regression results suggest that irrespective of government or railway land, slums located in non-notified area have significantly lower score.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to water supply (sufficiency and quality), sanitation (latrine/toilet), and drainage across 541 households in 23 slums of Kolkata.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — examines legal, administrative, institutional, and governance factors shaping basic service access, including municipal authorization of slums (notified vs. non-notified status), land title/encroachment (government land, railway land, and Thika Tenancy ownership), decentralized municipal service governance under the 74th Constitutional Amendment and West Bengal Municipal Act 1993, ward electoral competition and fragmentation, political clientelism, and caste/religious discrimination in municipal service delivery. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading: Yes — although electoral competition/fragmentation (VOTE, CONTEST, TCONTEST) and clientelism (HFLM) represent local political-economy governance rather than formal utility rules (and KEIP is a project-delivery dummy), the study explicitly operationalizes and empirically estimates settlement legal authorization and land-title/tenure status (non-notified/unauthorized slum NN vs. municipality-authorized notified slum, encroached government land GL, and encroached railway land RL) in cross-tabulations and four ordered probit models of household water, sanitation, and drainage access (IWSD), as well as discriminatory discretion/neglect toward minority and backward-caste households. Legal settlement notification and land-tenure/encroachment status fall directly within the protocol's rule-type mechanism scope (documentation or tenure requirements governing service access).
criterion_notes.c3: Primary quantitative empirical study based on a stratified cluster and systematic survey of 541 households in 23 slums of Kolkata, analyzed using descriptive statistics and maximum-likelihood ordered probit regressions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household-level outcomes for water supply sufficiency, water quality, access to sanitation (latrine/toilet), physical access to drainage and drain-cleaning frequency, and a composite Index of Water, Sanitation and Drainage (IWSD).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (541 slum households across 23 wards/slums in Kolkata), exposures (type of land title/notification status NN, GL, RL; ward political competition/clientelism; councillor and household social/religious identity), outcomes (water sufficiency, water quality, sanitation access, drainage access, and IWSD), and study design (cross-sectional household survey with ordered probit regression). Note that while the Appendix text detailing the exact weighting formula of IWSD components was omitted in the published PDF leaving Tables AI-AIV, review eligibility does not depend on synthesis-level effect extraction (Criterion 6 note), and both ordered probit estimates for IWSD and descriptive percentages for separate water and sanitation outcomes are reported.

study_design: Cross-sectional household survey (stratified cluster and systematic sampling) with ordered probit regression analysis
population_and_sample: 541 sample households selected via stratified cluster and systematic sampling from 23 slums (19 notified slums and 4 non-notified slums on government or railway land; 9% of households in non-notified slums) across 23 municipal wards in Kolkata, India (unit of analysis: household)
exposure: Legal slum notification and land-title/tenure status (non-notified/unauthorized slum NN vs. municipality-authorized notified slum; encroached government land GL and railway land RL), alongside ward electoral competition and fragmentation (VOTE, TCONTEST, CONTEST), political clientelism (HFLM), councillor identity/reelection (MC, REELEC), and household caste/religious identity (MUSLIM, SCST)
outcome: Household water supply sufficiency, water supply quality, access to sanitation (latrine/toilet), access to drainage and drain-cleaning frequency, and composite Index of Water, Sanitation and Drainage (IWSD)
rationale: This empirical household survey (n = 541 households across 23 slums in Kolkata, India) examines household access to water supply, sanitation (latrines), and drainage. In addition to analyzing child poverty, caste/religious disparities, and ward-level electoral competition and clientelism, the study explicitly defines, stratifies, and empirically models municipal legal authorization/notification and land-title status (notified/authorized slums vs. non-notified unauthorized slums encroaching on government land GL and railway land RL) as determinants of household water, sanitation, and drainage access using descriptive statistics and four ordered probit regression models. It therefore satisfies all inclusion criteria, including Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope (tenure and legal settlement-authorization requirements governing service access).
